title: Nine billion tokens, and the work behind the number
summary: What a shared platform’s throughput says—and what it leaves out.
content:
The shared AI platform behind the LiteLLM gateway I maintain and extend serves more than nine billion tokens a day. That is a useful way to communicate scale. It is also an incomplete way to describe the engineering.

A throughput number tells you that demand exists. It does not tell you whether a department can trace its usage, whether credentials stay within the right boundary, or whether a provider failure becomes a confusing error in someone else's application. Those questions determine whether the platform is usable.

## The number needs a denominator

Nine billion tokens belong to a shared platform, with shared effort behind it. My contribution sits in maintaining and extending the gateway: routing, failover, authentication, team isolation, budgets, and auditability. Keeping that distinction clear matters. A platform story should explain responsibility as carefully as it explains impact.

Consider two requests with identical token counts. One belongs to a classroom experiment; the other supports a departmental workflow. Their permissions, spending limits, and acceptable recovery behavior may differ. Aggregating them into one traffic chart hides the decisions that make each request legitimate.

## Follow one request

A useful architecture review starts with a single request. Which identity owns it? Which models may that identity use? What happens when the preferred provider is unavailable? Which records let an operator reconstruct the decision without storing unnecessary sensitive content?

Then widen the view. What happens when many teams make that request simultaneously? Can one busy workload consume another team's capacity? Does a retry create unexpected spend? Does the response still mean the same thing after a provider change?

These are less glamorous questions than a benchmark screenshot. They are also where a gateway earns trust.

## Make scale explainable

I want large numbers to lead to better questions, rather than end the conversation. Throughput, concurrency, and latency are useful observations. Ownership, isolation, and failure behavior explain whether those observations represent a dependable service.

The strongest version of the story is therefore specific: a shared platform with substantial demand, and a gateway that helps turn that demand into accountable access. The engineering work is in making the next request understandable, even when there are billions more behind it.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: An AI gateway is a policy boundary
summary: Routing a request is easy to draw. Deciding whether it should be routed takes more care.
content:
An AI gateway often appears in an architecture diagram as a small box between an application and a model provider. The box looks like plumbing. In practice, it is where a product's promises meet a platform's rules.

My work with LiteLLM includes provider routing, API-key authentication, role-based access, team isolation, budgets, and audit logs. These concerns belong together because access to a model is a decision about identity, resources, and responsibility.

## Start with the decision

Imagine a research tool submitting a request for a model that its team has not been authorized to use. The gateway could know how to route the request and still need to refuse it. A correct destination is only one part of a correct decision.

I find it useful to separate four questions: who is asking, what they may use, which resources they may consume, and what evidence of the decision should remain. Each question should have an owner and an explicit failure behavior.

For example, an unavailable authorization dependency should not silently become unrestricted access. A budget check should not disappear because the route takes a fallback path. A new provider should not accidentally bypass team restrictions inherited from the original request.

## Keep the policy legible

Complexity arrives when policy is scattered across clients, gateway configuration, and provider accounts. Two applications can appear to use the same service while enforcing different rules.

A central boundary can reduce that ambiguity, but centralization alone is not correctness. Configuration needs review, tests need to cover denials, and operators need to see why a decision happened. Successful requests are only half the test suite.

A practical review scenario is a key belonging to team A trying to access team B's resources. Another is a formerly authorized key after its permissions change. A third is a denied request during a provider outage. These cases expose accidental exceptions that happy-path demonstrations miss.

## Treat refusal as a product behavior

A rejection should carry enough information for the caller to respond appropriately, without revealing another team's configuration. The user needs a useful next action; the operator needs a traceable reason.

A gateway becomes valuable when these decisions remain coherent as providers and applications change. The routing box stays small on the diagram. Its responsibilities deserve considerably more space in the design document.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Failover should preserve the contract
summary: A backup provider is useful only when the application understands what changed.
content:
A fallback that returns a response can look like a reliability success. Whether it actually helped depends on what the caller expected from that response.

LiteLLM supports fallback model groups after failures and configured retries. That provides an important mechanism, but a mechanism is not the whole application contract. The model selected next may have different behavior, limits, or supported capabilities. The caller still needs an answer it can use. [LiteLLM's fallback documentation](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/reliability) describes the routing mechanism.

## Define compatibility before the outage

Consider an illustrative application that expects structured output with a particular schema. If its backup returns persuasive prose instead, the request may be technically successful while the workflow has failed. A second application may rely on a tool call that the backup handles differently. A third may be subject to data-routing restrictions.

The right fallback therefore starts with requirements: accepted output shape, required tools, data constraints, time budget, and cost boundary. A provider should qualify against those requirements before it becomes part of the recovery plan.

I would rather document a limited, explicit fallback than imply that every model is interchangeable.

## Partial output changes the problem

Before a response starts, switching providers can be relatively straightforward from the user's perspective. After content has been displayed, the application has a harder decision. Restarting may duplicate text or contradict the unfinished answer. Continuing with another model may not preserve the same context or meaning.

The interface should know whether it has a complete result, a recoverable interruption, or an incomplete artifact that needs a fresh attempt. A single generic success flag cannot express all three.

This is why testing only a provider's first-request failure leaves a gap. Failure after visible output deserves its own scenario.

## Budget the recovery

Retries and fallbacks also consume time and potentially money. A recovery chain should fit inside a request's overall deadline. Otherwise, the application can keep trying after the user has already abandoned it.

A dependable fallback is a deliberately narrower promise: if the preferred path fails under specified conditions, this alternate path can still satisfy these requirements. That promise is much easier to test than “the system always finds another model.” It is also more honest about the boundaries of resilience.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Streaming is a lifecycle, not a text effect
summary: The first token is the beginning of a conversation with the interface, not the end of the engineering.
content:
A streaming answer feels immediate because the user sees progress before the work is finished. Behind that effect sits a lifecycle: admission, execution, partial output, completion, interruption, and cleanup.

My real-time work includes Redis Pub/Sub, Celery, and server-sent events. The interesting part is not merely moving text across those components. It is keeping the browser's picture of the job consistent with what the system is doing.

## Give states names

An illustrative workflow might move through accepted, queued, running, streaming, and completed. It also needs cancelled and failed. These states should not be inferred solely from whether a connection is open.

An open connection can carry no useful work. A closed connection can follow a completed answer or an interrupted one. The client needs an explicit terminal event, and the server needs a clear rule about when that event is recorded.

SSE provides a browser-facing event format, including named events and event IDs. Those primitives help carry a lifecycle, but the application must define its semantics. [MDN's SSE guide](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events) is a useful reference for the transport.

## Separate work from observation

The worker owns execution. The browser observes it. That distinction becomes important when a tab closes or a connection drops.

Does the job continue? Can the user reconnect? Does cancellation mean stopping delivery, stopping the worker, or both? The answer depends on the workflow, but it should be explicit. Otherwise, “stop generating” can become a button that only hides activity while resources continue to run.

A job ID creates a stable identity across these changes. The connection is temporary; the job may outlive it.

## Close the loop

Completion should be durable enough for the interface to confirm what happened. Cleanup should release subscriptions and buffers. Failure should explain whether retrying starts a new job or resumes an existing one.

I like to review a streaming design by asking what happens if the browser disappears at every transition. That exercise makes hidden coupling visible quickly.

A polished stream is not one that never interrupts. It is one that can explain an interruption without losing the identity of the work. The typing effect is pleasant. The lifecycle is what makes it a system.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: The message you missed still matters
summary: Choosing a delivery mechanism means choosing what the system remembers.
content:
Redis Pub/Sub is useful when live listeners need immediate notifications. Its delivery model also places a clear boundary on what an application can assume: messages are delivered at most once, and a disconnected subscriber can miss them. [Redis documents this behavior explicitly](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/pubsub/).

That boundary matters when the notification describes something more consequential than a transient update.

## Separate notification from truth

Imagine a worker finishing a document-processing job while the browser briefly loses its connection. If the completion message exists only in Pub/Sub, the browser may keep displaying “processing” after the work is done.

The worker did its job. The notification mechanism did what it promised. The application still failed to reconcile them.

A durable job record can resolve that mismatch. The live message tells the client to look; the record tells the client what is true. On reconnect, the client reads the current state instead of assuming that every transition was observed.

This pattern does not make Pub/Sub durable. It gives durability a separate home.

## Decide which events require history

Some events are disposable. A progress indicator moving from 41 percent to 42 percent may not need to survive a disconnect if the latest state is available. A final result, permission change, or recorded operation may require stronger treatment.

I would classify events by the consequence of missing them, then choose delivery and storage accordingly. A single channel carrying everything can obscure those differences.

When replay is necessary, evaluate a durable event mechanism and its actual acknowledgment, retention, and consumer semantics. Do not label a system replayable merely because messages have IDs.

## Reconnection is part of normal operation

Connections drop for ordinary reasons: mobile networks, suspended tabs, deployment changes, and intermediate infrastructure. A reconnection path is therefore a primary workflow, not an obscure exception.

Test a listener that joins late. Test one that disconnects just before completion. Test duplicate notifications if the surrounding application may generate them. The important result is whether the client converges on the correct state.

The design question is simple: if nobody hears the message, does the system still know what happened? For work that matters, I want the answer to be yes.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Cancellation is resource management
summary: A stop button should have a meaning all the way through the stack.
content:
The user clicks stop. The text stops arriving. That is the visible part of cancellation, and it is easy to mistake it for the whole operation.

A worker may still be executing. A provider request may still be active. A subscription may remain registered. A result may arrive later and overwrite the state of a newer attempt. The interface can look calm while the system keeps spending resources.

## Define what stops

I would define cancellation separately for each layer: browser delivery, job execution, provider work, and persistence. Some layers may support immediate interruption; others may only stop at a safe checkpoint. The product should represent those limits accurately.

For an illustrative document workflow, a cancellation request during extraction could mean “finish the current file, then do not start another.” For a live response, it might mean “close delivery and attempt to stop generation.” Those are different promises.

The system should distinguish cancellation requested from cancellation confirmed when confirmation is not immediate.

## Protect the next attempt

A common race appears when a user cancels one request and starts another. The old result arrives late. If the interface identifies work only by the current loading flag, the obsolete result can be displayed as if it belongs to the new request.

A stable job identity and an explicit current-attempt check make that boundary visible. The browser accepts updates for the attempt it is observing. The server records each attempt separately. “Latest response wins” is a fragile substitute for ownership.

This matters even when cancellation cannot halt a remote operation. The application can still refuse to attach stale output to the wrong workflow.

## Review the cleanup

Cancellation should release listeners, timers, buffers, and temporary state. Cleanup needs to be safe when called more than once, because completion and cancellation can race.

The same review should ask what happens to partial artifacts. Are they retained for recovery, deleted, or marked incomplete? A document that looks finished but was interrupted halfway through is an avoidable source of confusion.

I think of cancellation as a small distributed protocol. The user expresses intent; components acknowledge it according to their capabilities; the interface shows the resulting state. A trustworthy stop button makes that protocol understandable instead of merely making the screen quiet.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: A retry needs a business key
summary: Queue delivery and application correctness answer different questions.
content:
Background workers make a request path simpler by moving long-running work elsewhere. They also force a question into the open: what happens when the same logical operation is attempted again?

Celery's task documentation discusses retries, acknowledgment choices, and the importance of idempotent tasks. Those mechanisms need to be matched to the application rather than treated as a universal safety switch. [The task guide](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html) explains the relevant worker behavior.

## Identify the operation

Consider an illustrative ingestion job that extracts a document, creates chunks, and stores embeddings. If the worker retries after the embeddings were written but before completion was recorded, a second execution could create duplicates.

A queue message ID identifies a delivery. A business key identifies the intended operation. Depending on the product, that key might include tenant, document version, and processing configuration. It should distinguish “retry the same work” from “process a genuinely new version.”

The database can then enforce the intended uniqueness instead of asking every worker to remember it perfectly.

## Split the side effects

External calls complicate idempotency. A transaction inside one database cannot roll back a request already accepted by another service.

I would make the stages explicit: acquire or inspect the operation record, perform a bounded unit of work, record the result, then advance. Each stage needs a recovery story for a worker disappearing immediately before or after its side effect.

This does not eliminate every race. It creates places where races can be reasoned about and tested.

A task that performs five unrelated effects and returns one success flag leaves too much ambiguity when it stops halfway through.

## Retry with purpose

Retries should target transient failures. Repeating a malformed request may add load without making progress. Repeating an unauthorized operation is worse. An operator should be able to see the failure classification and the attempt history.

Backoff, retry limits, and deadlines serve different purposes. A task can stay within its retry limit and still take longer than the workflow can tolerate.

The useful question is not “does the worker retry?” It is “can another attempt finish this operation without corrupting its meaning?” Once that answer is clear, the queue's delivery settings become implementation choices in a coherent design.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Backpressure is a product decision
summary: When demand exceeds capacity, the interface still owes the user a clear answer.
content:
A queue can absorb a burst. It cannot turn unlimited demand into unlimited capacity. At some point, an application must decide what happens to work it cannot process promptly.

That decision is often described as backpressure, but the user experiences it as waiting, rejection, reduced functionality, or an unexplained spinner. The system design and the product behavior are the same decision viewed from different ends.

## Count unfinished work

Request throughput alone can conceal a growing backlog. I would also inspect queue age, active jobs, processing time, and the rate at which work completes. A busy system can look healthy while every new request waits longer than the last.

The useful boundary is often a limit on unfinished work, not simply requests arriving per second. Long jobs occupy capacity differently from short ones. Separate workload classes may need separate queues or quotas.

Otherwise, a small number of expensive jobs can make an ordinary interactive request feel broken.

## Choose a visible policy

For an illustrative analysis tool, the policy might be: admit work while the expected wait is acceptable, show a queue state when it is not immediate, and reject additional work once the queue reaches a defined limit.

The exact thresholds need measurement. The important part is that the application has a policy rather than an accidental timeout.

A rejection should say whether the user can retry, whether their input was retained, and whether any operation actually began. A queued request should have an identity and a cancellation path. The browser should not encourage repeated submissions that worsen the backlog.

## Protect useful work

Fairness becomes important on a shared platform. One team's batch workload should not silently consume the capacity intended for another team's interactive use. Budgets, concurrency controls, and scheduling rules can make those boundaries explicit.

Load testing should therefore include mixed workloads, not only a stream of identical requests. The question is whether the system protects the behavior it promised to each class of user.

I want overload to be legible. A service that clearly says “not yet” can be more dependable than one that accepts everything and fails much later. Backpressure is where engineering decides which promises it can still keep under pressure.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Latency needs a story, not just a percentile
summary: A number becomes useful when it explains where the user spent their time.
content:
A latency percentile is a compact summary of many requests. It can reveal a regression or help define a target. It can also flatten several different experiences into one number.

A streaming answer, a document import, and a dashboard refresh do not have the same definition of “done.” Treating their latency as interchangeable makes a metric easier to display and harder to use.

## Name the interval

For a streaming workflow, I want to distinguish time to acceptance, time waiting for execution, time to first useful output, and time to completion. For a document pipeline, extraction and indexing deserve separate observations.

A fast first token can coexist with a slow complete answer. A quick API acknowledgment can hide a long queue. Neither measurement is wrong; each describes a different interval.

The metric name should carry that distinction. “Response time” is too broad when the system returns an acknowledgment and continues working elsewhere.

## Explain the distribution

Percentiles are most useful alongside request volume, errors, and workload shape. A comparison between two periods may reflect a different mix of documents or model requests rather than a code improvement.

I would segment by meaningful workload characteristics before drawing a conclusion. That might include route, processing stage, or a bounded size category. It should not require exposing sensitive inputs or creating unbounded metric labels.

A trace can then explain an individual path through the system. OpenTelemetry describes traces as a representation of a request's journey through operations; that is a useful complement to an aggregate chart. [Its tracing concepts](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/) explain the relationship.

## Connect the number to a decision

An observation should suggest an action. If queue wait dominates, optimizing JSON serialization may not help. If retrieval is fast but generation is slow, changing the database index may solve the wrong problem.

I still value percentile improvements. I simply want them attached to a workflow, a measurement boundary, and a reason the change matters.

For a personal project or a production platform, the best performance story is not a lone number in large type. It is an explanation of what got faster, what remained expensive, and how that changed the experience of the person waiting.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Retrieval can fail before the model speaks
summary: A fluent answer cannot repair evidence that never reached the prompt.
content:
A retrieval-augmented application can produce a confident answer while making its most important mistake earlier in the pipeline. The relevant document was never retrieved, the useful passage was split badly, or an access filter removed the wrong material.

The model then answers from the evidence it received. Fluency makes the result look complete, even when the evidence was incomplete.

## Inspect the evidence separately

My work includes document pipelines, hybrid retrieval, reranking, and source attribution. I find those pieces easier to reason about when retrieval quality is evaluated before answer quality.

For an illustrative policy question, first identify the passages that should be available to an authorized user. Then inspect whether retrieval returns them, how highly they rank, and whether the returned text includes the necessary qualification.

Only after that should the generated answer be judged. Otherwise, a poor answer can send the investigation toward prompting when the real issue is extraction or indexing.

## Preserve the question's shape

Some questions depend on exact terms: a course code, an identifier, a date, or a named exception. Others depend on meaning expressed differently from the document. A retrieval strategy needs to account for those differences.

A useful evaluation set includes both. It should also include questions whose answer is absent, questions requiring several passages, and questions that should return different evidence for different authorized users.

A system that always returns something can hide the difference between relevance and availability. Empty evidence is sometimes the correct result.

## Keep a record of the decision

For debugging, I want a bounded record of the retrieval process: query configuration, document versions, filters, selected passage identifiers, and scores with their meaning documented. Sensitive document contents do not need to become unrestricted logs.

That record lets an engineer ask whether a failure came from stale data, poor candidate selection, access policy, or answer construction. Without it, changing the prompt becomes an attractive but poorly targeted experiment.

The application earns trust when it can distinguish “I found supporting evidence” from “I generated a plausible response.” Retrieval is not an invisible prelude to intelligence. It is the process that decides what the answer is allowed to know.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Hybrid search needs two ways to be right
summary: Exact wording and semantic similarity catch different failures.
content:
A document can be relevant because it contains the exact term in a question. It can also be relevant because it describes the same idea using different words. Neither signal covers every case.

That is the attraction of hybrid retrieval: preserve more than one way for useful evidence to become a candidate.

## Keep the strengths distinct

An illustrative query for an internal reference number needs exact matching to matter. A query phrased as “how do I restore access after leaving a team?” may need passages that use different language. Dense similarity and lexical retrieval approach those cases differently.

Combining candidates does not mean their raw scores are directly comparable. The ranking design needs a deliberate fusion strategy or another documented method. Otherwise, one score range can dominate for numerical reasons rather than relevance.

The pgvector project discusses combining vector search with PostgreSQL full-text search and points to rank-fusion approaches. [Its hybrid-search section](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#hybrid-search) is a useful starting reference.

## Evaluate the hard queries

I would build a small test set with exact identifiers, abbreviations, paraphrases, negations, and ambiguous terms. Each query should have an expected evidence set, including cases where no answer is available.

The interesting result is not simply a higher average score. It is which failure classes improved and which became worse. A configuration that helps broad conceptual questions may bury a precise match under many similar passages.

Reranking can help sort candidates, but it adds another stage whose behavior and cost need measurement. Candidate selection and final ordering should be inspected separately.

## Respect filters throughout

Tenant and permission filters belong in every retrieval path. A lexical branch and a vector branch that apply different access rules create a serious inconsistency, even if their final ranking looks excellent.

I also want the displayed citations to preserve document identity through fusion and reranking. The answer should not lose the connection to the source while the search pipeline rearranges candidates.

Hybrid search is valuable because it accepts that relevance has several signals. The engineering challenge is to combine those signals without hiding their tradeoffs. Better retrieval starts with understanding why each candidate was allowed into the conversation.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Chunking is a document design problem
summary: The unit you index should preserve the unit a reader needs to understand.
content:
A fixed chunk size is convenient. Documents are rarely written in fixed units of meaning.

A heading introduces a section. A table depends on its column labels. An exception modifies a rule in the previous paragraph. A footnote may change the interpretation of a number. Splitting these relationships can make a perfectly extracted document difficult to retrieve correctly.

## Preserve useful boundaries

For an illustrative handbook, I would prefer a passage that carries its section heading and the qualification attached to its rule. The goal is not to make every chunk large. It is to keep the context needed to interpret a retrieved passage.

For a spreadsheet-derived document, a row without column names is often an incomplete fact. For an invoice, a value without its label is ambiguous. For a multi-page table, the page boundary may be less meaningful than the table boundary.

Chunking should therefore start with document structure where that structure is available.

## Treat extraction as a separate source of error

OCR fallback can make scanned material searchable, but extraction errors can distort both retrieval and answers. An identifier with one wrong character may defeat exact search. A reordered table may turn the right values into the wrong relationships.

I would retain extraction method and document version as metadata, then test representative scanned and digital documents separately. A chunking change should not be credited with solving a problem that actually came from better extraction.

Likewise, more overlap may recover missing context while increasing redundancy. It is a tradeoff to measure, not an automatic improvement.

## Review the retrieved passage as a reader

A useful manual test is to hide the original document and read only the retrieved chunk. Can a person understand what it claims? Can they identify its subject, scope, and qualifications? Can they follow a citation back to the surrounding material?

That test catches problems a token-count report cannot.

I think of chunking as preparing evidence for a reader who may arrive out of order. The system is responsible for giving that reader enough context to interpret what was found. Good boundaries make retrieval more useful before a model writes a single sentence.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: A citation should be inspectable
summary: A source link is useful when a reader can verify the claim it accompanies.
content:
A citation can improve an answer's appearance without improving its accountability. A link to a large document is technically a source, but it may leave the reader searching through hundreds of pages to find the relevant evidence.

The real value of a citation is the path it creates from a claim to material that supports that claim.

## Carry identity through the pipeline

A retrieved passage should retain document identity, version, and a useful location. The answer can then point to the same evidence the system actually used.

In an illustrative document assistant, that location might be a page number and passage identifier. In a spreadsheet assistant, it could be a sheet name and row range. The appropriate form depends on the source, but “somewhere in this file” is a weak destination.

The source should also remain accessible to the user who receives the answer. A citation to evidence they cannot open creates an apparent explanation without a practical verification path.

## Match claims to evidence

An answer may combine a fact from one passage with an interpretation from another. Those relationships should not collapse into a list of links at the end.

I would review citations claim by claim: does this passage support this statement, does it include the relevant qualification, and is the statement stronger than the evidence? A correct link can still accompany an overstated conclusion.

Evaluation should include misleading citations, unsupported claims with plausible links, and answers that cite an outdated document version. Merely counting source markers will miss these cases.

## Allow uncertainty to stay visible

Sometimes the available material does not resolve a question. The answer can name the gap instead of decorating a guess with a citation.

A useful response might explain that the document describes a general rule but does not specify how it applies to the user's case. That keeps interpretation separate from evidence and gives the user a better next step.

My preferred citation experience is simple: a reader can move from answer to passage, understand why it was selected, and decide whether it supports the claim. The link is an invitation to inspect the reasoning, not a badge declaring that the reasoning is finished.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Permissions belong before generation
summary: A document assistant should retrieve only what the user is allowed to know.
content:
A document assistant can be careful in its wording and still expose information through the evidence it retrieves. Once restricted material enters the context, asking the model not to reveal it is a weak place to put the boundary.

Access decisions belong before generation, and they need to remain consistent through every retrieval stage.

## Make ownership explicit

An illustrative internal assistant might serve several departments. Each document needs a tenant or ownership boundary, a version, and an access policy that the retrieval system can enforce.

The query needs the corresponding identity context. That context should come from trusted authentication and authorization state rather than a user-editable instruction such as “I belong to finance.”

Candidate retrieval, reranking, cached answers, and source links should all respect the same boundary. A secure vector query does not help if a cached response was created under another user's permissions.

## Test denials as carefully as answers

A useful test asks an authorized user for a restricted fact, then repeats the same query under a different identity. The expected evidence changes, even though the words of the query do not.

Another test changes permissions after a response has been cached. A third checks a document that moved between groups or acquired a new version. These scenarios expose assumptions about ownership that a static demonstration cannot.

The test should inspect retrieved identifiers as well as the final answer. A model declining to repeat restricted text does not prove that retrieval enforced the boundary.

## Keep debugging bounded

Engineers need to understand why evidence was included or excluded. That does not require copying every restricted passage into general-purpose logs.

Useful records can include policy decisions, document identifiers, and filter configuration under appropriate access controls. The principle is to preserve enough evidence for diagnosis without creating an unintended second distribution channel for the underlying content.

A retrieval system is part of the application's security model. It should behave like a data-access layer with explicit permissions, not a neutral search box followed by a polite model. The strongest protection is to avoid handing the wrong evidence to the model in the first place.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Evals are executable product expectations
summary: A good evaluation suite explains what the application promises to do.
content:
An evaluation score is useful only when its meaning survives a conversation with the person using the application. “Quality improved” needs a more concrete explanation: the assistant found the relevant passage more often, stopped inventing unsupported details, or produced output that the next system could actually accept.

My evaluation work spans retrieval relevance, groundedness, tool-call correctness, schema conformance, latency, and provider failures. I think of these as separate expectations rather than one interchangeable measure of intelligence.

## Give each case a reason to exist

An illustrative test case should include an input, expected behavior, and a description of the failure it is meant to catch. A query about an absent fact might require an explicit statement that the evidence does not answer it. A tool request might require the correct argument values and a refusal to call an unauthorized operation.

This makes a failure actionable. The engineer can see which promise changed instead of trying to interpret a composite score.

I would include ordinary cases, boundary cases, and cases with insufficient evidence. A test set made entirely of easy successes encourages a system that appears capable until it reaches the first ambiguous request.

## Version the environment

A result depends on more than the prompt. Document versions, retrieval configuration, tool schemas, model settings, and evaluation logic can all affect it.

Recording those inputs allows a comparison to explain what changed. Without that record, a regression can be indistinguishable from a different dataset or a moving dependency.

For probabilistic output, repeatability also needs an honest definition. A single favorable run is a weak basis for declaring a general improvement.

## Keep judgment visible

Some checks are deterministic: valid schema, expected identifier, prohibited tool call. Others require human assessment or a carefully designed evaluator. Those categories should remain distinct in the report.

I want the evaluation suite to help a reviewer understand the application, not just approve a release. Its cases should read like a map of the promises the product makes.

The best scorecard therefore has a narrative behind it: these are the workflows we care about, these are the failures we refuse to hide, and this change improves these expectations under these conditions.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Valid JSON is not a valid decision
summary: A response can satisfy a schema and still misunderstand the task.
content:
Structured output makes an AI response easier to pass into software. It does not make the response correct.

A payload can contain every required field and still refer to the wrong account, choose an unsupported action, or express confidence where the evidence is missing. Syntax is one layer of the contract. Meaning is another.

## Validate in stages

I would separate parsing, structural validation, domain validation, and authorization. Parsing establishes whether the payload can be read. A schema establishes shape and types. Domain rules establish whether the values make sense together. Authorization establishes whether the requested operation is allowed.

Pydantic's model documentation describes validation and the resulting model guarantees; the application still needs rules appropriate to its domain. [The models guide](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/) is useful for understanding that boundary.

Consider an illustrative scheduling response. A well-formed start time and end time are not enough if the end precedes the start. A legitimate project ID is not enough if it belongs to another team. A tool name is not enough if the user never authorized the action.

## Return useful failures

A validation failure should help the caller distinguish a malformed response from a prohibited operation or an unresolved request. Those cases need different recovery behavior.

Blindly asking the model to try again can turn a clear authorization denial into a repeated attempt. Repairing formatting may be appropriate for a parse error, but it should not silently revise the user's intended action.

The system needs to preserve the original request and the validation reason through any repair path.

## Evaluate the accepted mistakes

Tests often focus on invalid payloads because they are easy to reject. I also want examples that are structurally valid and semantically wrong.

These cases reveal whether the application is treating schema conformance as a substitute for understanding. They are especially important when structured output becomes input to another service rather than text reviewed by a person.

The practical goal is a layered boundary: make the output readable, make its values meaningful, then decide whether it may be used. JSON is a transport format. It should never become the entire argument for trusting an operation.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: A tool call needs intent, not just arguments
summary: Knowing how to call an operation is different from knowing whether to call it.
content:
An agent can produce the correct tool name and perfectly formatted arguments while taking the wrong action. The missing piece is often intent: did the user ask for this operation, and do they understand its consequence?

This question is central to the kind of risk review I explore in IntentGuard. The project gathers command context and explains risk before a confirm-or-abort decision. It is an alpha exploration, not a guarantee that every hazardous operation can be recognized.

## Separate advice from execution

An illustrative request to explain a cleanup command should not become permission to run that command. A request to inspect a deployment should not automatically become permission to replace it.

The application needs a distinction between reading state, preparing a change, and executing a consequential action. Tool schemas describe available operations; they do not establish authorization for each use.

A useful interface can make the proposed action concrete before asking for confirmation: target, scope, expected effect, and the relevant uncertainty. “Proceed?” without those details asks the user to approve a guess.

## Context changes the risk

The same command can have different consequences depending on its directory, arguments, environment, and target. Reviewing isolated text misses much of that context.

I would preserve enough surrounding state to explain why a command deserves scrutiny. That includes resolved paths and the nature of the operation, while avoiding unnecessary collection of sensitive content.

The explanation should identify the consequence in plain language. A technical label such as “high risk” is less useful than “this removes the selected directory and everything inside it.”

## Evaluate the boundary

A test suite should include ambiguous intent, requests for explanation, approved actions, and attempts that exceed the approved scope. It should inspect whether an operation was proposed or executed, not just whether the generated explanation sounded cautious.

False reassurance is an important failure mode. So is unnecessary interruption for every harmless step.

The goal is a well-placed decision boundary. An agent should help the user understand a meaningful action, obtain the authority it actually needs, and keep execution within that authority. Calling the right function is only one part of that responsibility.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: A prompt builder is a workflow editor
summary: The useful artifact is a repeatable task, not a clever sentence.
content:
A prompt builder can easily become a large text area with a decorative “improve” button. The harder product is a place where someone can understand, test, and maintain a repeatable task.

I led NaviGator Prompt Builder using Next.js, TypeScript, and FastAPI. That work sits at the intersection I enjoy: interface design, backend contracts, and AI behavior that needs to remain understandable to the person using it.

## Surface the moving parts

A useful workflow separates instructions, variables, source material, output expectations, and execution settings. When everything is buried in one paragraph, changing a single assumption can have consequences the user cannot see.

An illustrative department workflow might summarize incoming reports. Its reusable instructions should be distinct from the report being summarized. Its expected output should be explicit. Its test examples should include a report with missing information.

These distinctions make the task easier to review and reduce the temptation to treat every bad result as a wording problem.

## Make revision observable

A user should be able to compare versions and understand what changed. The comparison needs more than a diff of prose: did the output contract change, did a variable become required, or did the workflow gain access to another tool?

A saved configuration should retain the settings needed to reproduce a test. Otherwise, yesterday's successful example becomes a memory rather than evidence.

I also want the interface to distinguish a draft from a tested version. Saving text is not the same event as validating behavior.

## Design for the next maintainer

The author may understand every abbreviation and exception when creating the workflow. Someone else may inherit it months later.

A short purpose statement, representative examples, and visible constraints make that handoff easier. The interface should encourage those artifacts instead of demanding that every user become an expert in prompting vocabulary.

The interesting product question is therefore not “how do we make instructions sound better?” It is “how do we help someone build a task they can explain and revise safely?”

A strong prompt builder leaves behind more than a prompt. It leaves behind a small, inspectable workflow with a purpose, a contract, and evidence of how it behaves.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: IntentGuard and the space before Enter
summary: A command review tool should turn uncertainty into an understandable decision.
content:
The moment before a command runs is a useful place to intervene. The text is visible, the target can still be inspected, and the user can choose a different action before anything changes.

IntentGuard is my alpha Python and LiteLLM CLI project exploring that moment. It gathers context, explains potentially risky commands, and offers a confirm-or-abort decision. The interesting challenge is making the explanation useful without pretending that an AI review can prove a command safe.

## Explain the consequence

A warning that says “dangerous command detected” leaves too much work to the reader. A better explanation identifies what the command targets and what it may change.

For an illustrative recursive deletion, the resolved directory matters more than the scary appearance of the syntax. For a deployment command, the environment and replacement behavior matter. For a pipeline, the input and destination can alter the consequence.

The tool should therefore explain the evidence it used and the uncertainty it could not resolve. Missing context should remain visible rather than being filled in with confidence.

## Keep approval concrete

A user should confirm an action they can inspect. The reviewed command, its arguments, and its relevant context need to correspond to the operation that would execute.

If the command changes after review, the earlier explanation may no longer apply. If the directory changes, a relative path can refer to something else. These details turn command review into a question about binding a decision to a specific operation.

A helpful alpha project should make these boundaries explicit in its design and documentation.

## Measure more than detection

I would evaluate missed hazards, incorrect warnings, ambiguous explanations, and scope changes after review. An excellent-looking explanation of the wrong target is still a failure.

The cost of unnecessary interruption also matters. A tool that asks for approval constantly trains people to stop reading.

What interests me about IntentGuard is the combination of developer tooling and human judgment. The system can gather context and explain it quickly. The user needs a clear, bounded choice. The space before Enter is small, but it is large enough to make an action more deliberate.

[Explore IntentGuard](https://github.com/saisriharsha19/IntentGuard).
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: WebLMS and the boundary of a tab
summary: Contextual assistance starts with deciding what page context to use.
content:
A browser assistant is close to useful context. It is also close to information the user did not necessarily intend to share.

WebLMS explores contextual chat using browser extensions, DOM and OCR extraction, client-side privacy filters, and a FastAPI and Redis backend. The design question that interests me most is how to make the context boundary visible.

## Select before sending

A page can include the material a user wants to discuss alongside navigation, unrelated messages, account details, and hidden interface elements. “Use the current page” is a broad instruction unless the product explains what it includes.

I would want the user to inspect the selected context and narrow it before a request. The browser can do useful filtering locally, but the interface should still make the resulting selection understandable.

OCR expands what can be extracted. It also adds uncertainty about recognition and layout. The assistant should not treat every extracted string as equally reliable.

## Keep context attached to its origin

An answer based on a page needs to preserve where the relevant material came from. A title, source URL, or visible excerpt can help the user tell whether the assistant is discussing the intended document.

If the tab navigates, the previous context should not silently become context for the new page. The conversation may continue, but the application needs a clear rule for whether it retains, replaces, or asks to refresh its source.

That is a workflow decision, not merely a caching detail.

## Design privacy as interaction

Privacy filters are useful, but a promise that “sensitive content is removed” is broader than any imperfect filter can justify. The stronger design combines limited collection, visible selection, explicit submission, and careful handling of retained context.

Testing should include pages with mixed content, extraction failures, and navigation during an active request. These cases reveal whether the system understands the boundary it presents to the user.

The browser is a compelling place to build assistance because the user's task is already there. WebLMS is an exploration of using that proximity carefully: enough context to help, enough visibility for the user to decide what assistance should know.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Forecasting starts with a data contract
summary: A model cannot repair a time series whose meaning changes between rows.
content:
A forecast can arrive with a clean chart while resting on a poorly defined series. Before choosing a forecasting model, I want to know what each observation means.

My departmental data-science work includes Excel and PDF inputs, large tabular datasets, and TimesFM forecasting. Those ingredients make data preparation part of the modeling problem, not a preliminary chore.

## Define the observation

An illustrative weekly service-demand series needs a consistent time interval, unit, and aggregation rule. Does a missing week mean zero demand or missing data? Did a category change its definition? Were historical records revised?

These questions influence the series before any model sees it. Filling a missing value with zero may create an artificial event. Combining categories with different meanings may produce a tidy number that no longer answers the original question.

The pipeline should preserve the choices made during cleaning and aggregation.

## Separate observation from prediction

A chart should distinguish recorded values from forecast values. If uncertainty is available and appropriate to the method, it should be represented with its meaning explained. A precise-looking line should not imply a certainty the workflow has not established.

I would also make the forecast horizon explicit. A model evaluated for short horizons should not inherit an untested promise about much longer ones.

The user needs to understand the question the chart answers, not just admire its smoothness.

## Evaluate in time order

A useful forecast evaluation respects the order in which information would have become available. An illustrative test can train or condition on an earlier period and assess a later one, repeating that process across several cutoffs.

A baseline matters. If a simple seasonal or recent-value approach performs similarly, the added complexity needs another justification. The result should explain errors in terms meaningful to the workflow, not only in terms of a convenient metric.

For me, the interesting work is making a forecast accountable to its input. The model contributes a prediction. The application contributes definitions, provenance, evaluation, and presentation. Without those pieces, an impressive chart can be a polished answer to a question nobody actually agreed on.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Data agents should show their work
summary: A numerical answer needs a route back to the rows that produced it.
content:
A natural-language interface makes a large dataset easier to approach. It also makes it easier to hide the steps between a question and a number.

My work on a departmental Data Science Agent includes large Excel and PDF inputs, retrieval, and analysis workflows. The product challenge is to let a user ask a broad question while preserving enough detail to verify the result.

## Make the transformation visible

For an illustrative question such as “which department changed most this quarter?”, the answer depends on definitions. Which records count? What defines the quarter? Is the comparison absolute or relative? How are missing values handled?

A useful response should reveal those choices. It can include the selected dataset version, relevant columns, filters, aggregation, and a compact result table. The user should not have to infer the calculation from a fluent paragraph.

If a question is ambiguous, clarification can be more valuable than immediate computation.

## Distinguish search from calculation

Retrieval can find a relevant sheet, definition, or explanatory passage. Arithmetic still needs a controlled computational path. A language model's summary should not become the only record of how a numerical result was obtained.

I would retain an inspectable transformation or query where appropriate, with boundaries on execution and access. The answer can then describe a result computed by a defined process rather than presenting an unsupported estimate.

This distinction is particularly useful when evidence spans both narrative documents and tables.

## Keep the evidence small enough to inspect

Showing every row is not the same as making the work understandable. A concise table, row count, and explanation of exclusions may be more useful than a giant dump.

The interface should let the user drill down when necessary while keeping the main answer readable. Sensitive records still need the same permission boundaries as any other data-access workflow.

The goal is not to make every user inspect every operation. It is to make inspection possible when the result matters. A data agent becomes more useful when it can answer both “what is the result?” and “how did you get there?”
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Health checks are promises
summary: A running process is not always a service ready to accept work.
content:
A health endpoint can return a reassuring response while the application cannot perform its useful function. The endpoint is working; the promise behind it is underspecified.

Kubernetes separates startup, readiness, and liveness probes. Readiness influences whether a pod receives traffic, while liveness can trigger a restart. These distinctions are central to choosing meaningful checks. [The Kubernetes probe documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/) explains their behavior.

## Ask different questions

Startup asks whether the application has finished beginning. Readiness asks whether it can accept work now. Liveness asks whether restarting the process is an appropriate response to its condition.

Those questions should not automatically use the same test. A dependency outage may make a service temporarily unable to fulfill some requests without making a restart useful. Repeated restarts can add disruption to a condition the process cannot fix.

An expensive readiness check can also become part of the workload it is meant to protect. The check should be purposeful and bounded.

## Define the useful function

For an illustrative API, readiness might depend on configuration being loaded and the minimum required resources being available. For a worker, health may involve its ability to make progress rather than its ability to answer an HTTP request.

The right signal depends on the service. Copying a health endpoint from another project can copy the wrong assumption about what healthy means.

I would document each check's consequence alongside its implementation. That makes it easier to review whether a failure should remove traffic, restart a container, or alert an operator.

## Test the failure behavior

A deployment test should include slow startup, temporary dependency failure, and a process that remains alive but stops doing useful work. The important observation is what the platform does in response.

Rollouts also need a clear connection between readiness and user-visible availability. A passing probe should mean enough to justify sending the next request.

Health checks are small pieces of code with large operational consequences. Their value comes from a specific promise: this signal means this service can do this kind of work, and this failure warrants this response. That promise deserves more attention than a generic “OK.”
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Query tuning starts with the question
summary: The fastest query is unhelpful if it computes the wrong thing.
content:
My earlier systems-engineering work included PostgreSQL and MSSQL query tuning. The habit I want to preserve from that work is simple: understand the query's purpose before trying to make its execution faster.

A slow endpoint can invite a quick index change. Sometimes that helps. Sometimes the query is doing more work than the product actually needs.

## Write down the intended result

An illustrative dashboard may request all historical records when it displays only the most recent page. Another endpoint may join a large table only to confirm that one related record exists. A third may repeat the same lookup for every item.

Before choosing an optimization, I would define the exact result and inspect the path that produces it. Pagination, filtering, and aggregation choices can change the amount of work more substantially than a local implementation tweak.

Correctness remains the first constraint. An index does not rescue an incorrect join.

## Inspect the plan

PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN documentation describes how to inspect the planner's chosen execution plan, including estimates and actual execution details when requested. That information helps replace intuition with evidence. [The official guide](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html) is the appropriate reference.

I would compare estimated and observed work, identify where rows expand or filters remove them, and account for realistic data distribution. A plan that works on a tiny development dataset may behave differently on a populated system.

Measurements should also preserve the workload conditions used for comparison.

## Include the application

The database is one part of the endpoint. Serialization, repeated calls, network waits, and downstream services can dominate after a query improves.

A useful performance story therefore follows the request through the application as well as the database. Otherwise, a large query improvement can have a surprisingly small effect on the user's wait.

I like optimizations that make the system easier to explain: fewer unnecessary rows, clearer joins, deliberate indexes, and a result contract that matches the interface. Speed is the observable benefit. Understanding why the system did less work is what makes the benefit maintainable.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: An ETL pipeline should preserve an explanation
summary: A transformed dataset is more useful when its history remains visible.
content:
An ETL pipeline is often described as three verbs: extract, transform, load. The description leaves out a fourth responsibility: explain.

My public-data projects include the FBI Data Pipeline and real-time incident-processing work. What interests me in these systems is the path from source material to a result someone can interpret.

## Keep provenance with the data

An illustrative public dataset may change its fields, revise historical records, or arrive with missing periods. A transformed row should retain enough provenance to identify its source version and the transformation that produced it.

Without that information, a discrepancy becomes difficult to investigate. The pipeline may have changed, the source may have changed, or the analyst may be comparing different definitions.

A timestamp alone is often insufficient. The processing configuration and source identity matter too.

## Make invalid records visible

Dropping a malformed record can keep a pipeline running. Quietly dropping many records can make the output misleading.

I would account for input counts, accepted records, rejected records, and the reasons for rejection. A useful error path preserves enough information to diagnose a problem under appropriate access controls.

The goal is not to halt every batch for every anomaly. It is to prevent “success” from concealing an incomplete result.

Schema changes deserve the same treatment. A renamed field should not silently become a column full of null values.

## Build for replay

A replay should have a defined meaning. Does it replace a partition, append records, or update existing ones? How does the pipeline distinguish a corrected source from a duplicate delivery?

Those decisions connect ETL design to idempotency and versioning. A reproducible transformation is easier to validate when its inputs and configuration are explicit.

For public data, presentation matters as well. A chart should communicate the dataset's scope and limitations rather than implying that every missing record represents a real-world absence.

The final table is an artifact. The pipeline's explanation is what lets someone trust that artifact, investigate it, and rebuild it when the source changes. Good ETL carries its history forward instead of leaving it behind in a job log.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Compiler design makes boundaries concrete
summary: Parsing, meaning, and execution become easier to reason about when they are separate.
content:
My compiler-design project explores a Delphi-Pascal interpreter using Java and ANTLR. It is a useful counterweight to work with probabilistic systems: the language has explicit structure, and the implementation has to decide what that structure means.

The part I find especially interesting is the separation between parsing a program and executing it.

## A parse is not an interpretation

An expression can be syntactically valid while referring to an undefined name or applying an operation to an inappropriate value. Recognizing the grammar is only one stage.

An abstract syntax tree gives the program a structure the implementation can inspect. Name resolution, type rules, and execution semantics can then be considered without treating the source as an undifferentiated string.

This separation makes failures more precise. “Unexpected token” and “undefined variable” describe different problems and should lead to different explanations.

## Small programs expose large choices

An illustrative assignment looks simple until scope becomes involved. Does a name refer to the local environment or an outer one? What happens when a declaration shadows another? When is a value read, and where is an update stored?

Arithmetic introduces another set of choices: value types, conversion rules, and errors. Control flow brings questions about evaluation order and termination.

These are not obscure implementation details. They determine the meaning of the program the user wrote.

## Carry the lesson elsewhere

The same habit is useful in API design and AI workflows. Parse the input, validate its structure, establish its meaning, then decide what may execute. Each stage should have a contract and a useful error.

A tool call encoded as JSON still needs interpretation. A retrieved passage still needs context. A valid configuration still needs domain rules.

Compiler work makes those boundaries concrete because the implementation cannot rely on a persuasive explanation to cover an ambiguous rule. It must choose and implement a behavior.

I value projects that train this kind of precision. An interpreter is not only a way to execute a language. It is a way to practice turning an idea into explicit semantics, one small program at a time.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati

title: Motion should explain, not compete
summary: An interface can feel alive without moving the things a person is trying to read.
content:
A personal website should communicate personality. Animation can help, but moving text and a shifting portrait can make the page harder to use precisely when someone is trying to learn about the person behind it.

This site's motion direction is intentionally restrained: the reading surface stays still, while small project diagrams can show a process. The distinction gives motion a job.

## Keep the reading surface stable

A heading should not need to finish an entrance effect before it becomes legible. A photograph should not drift while someone studies it. A card should not blur its text as the pointer moves.

These effects may look striking in a short recording, but the website is primarily a reading experience. Stability helps the visitor scan, compare projects, and decide where to go next.

Color, spacing, typography, and composition can carry much of the visual identity without requiring constant movement.

## Give each animation a meaning

A retrieval diagram can suggest evidence moving toward an answer. A streaming diagram can show events passing through stages. A compiler diagram can show source becoming structure.

The animation should stay inside the illustration rather than moving the surrounding layout. It should be slow enough to understand, limited in scope, and easy to pause.

A shared animation applied to every project may create consistency while communicating nothing about the projects. A small, distinct diagram can explain more with less motion.

## Respect the visitor's control

Reduced-motion preferences should change the experience meaningfully. MDN documents the prefers-reduced-motion media feature for detecting that preference. [Its reference](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/prefers-reduced-motion) explains the browser signal.

A visible pause control is also useful for visitors who want to stop a diagram temporarily. Offscreen animation can pause because it is not helping anyone understand the page at that moment.

I want the site to feel considered rather than restless. The best motion contributes to a question the visitor is already asking: what does this project do? When an effect cannot answer that question or improve feedback, a still composition is often the stronger design choice.
author: Sai Sri Harsha Guddati
